newsitem.title: GERMANY: Study warns EMU delay would hit German economy.
newsitem.headline: Study warns EMU delay would hit German economy.

text.p: Delaying introduction of Europe's planned single currency by just one year would put a damper on German economic growth and abandoning the project altogether would have dire consequences, an economic study said on Monday.

A study by the Frankfurt-based Wefa institute, commissioned by news weekly Focus for the magazine's latest edition, said delay of the euro by one year would cost 130,000 jobs and a decline in economic growth of 0.7 percent in 1998.

Should the ambitious European economic and monetary union (EMU) planned for 1999 be abandoned, German companies would slash domestic investment by as much as 60 billion marks and 800,000 jobs would be lost by the year 2002, the study said.

The report said that financial markets have been speculating since 1995 that the euro would come on time in 1999 and that so-called "Club Med" nations Italy, Spain, Portugal would be among the first wave of EMU nations.
Should this wager fail as a result of a delay or cancellation of EMU, huge volumes of funds would flow out of these countries and into the mark, causing a sharp appreciation of the German currency.
The resulting strength of the mark against other currencies would put German industry at a competitive disadvantage, particularly in Europe, where 40 percent of its exports go.
"Should the euro be delayed or buried this speculation bubble will burst," said Focus. "The result: a European economic crisis."
The Bonn government has long said failure or delay of EMU would most likely lead to a sharp appreciation of the mark and have negative consequences for the German economy.

Critics of Germany's handling of the EMU debate say Chancellor Helmut Kohl is painting a doom and gloom scenario that sees Europe reverting to the days of hostile nationalism should the currency project fail.

While warning of the impact of a delay in EMU, Bonn has insisted that all participants must strictly adhere to the fiscal criteria set out in the Maastricht Treaty, particularly the budget deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product.
But German industry and financial markets appear more concerned about the impact of a delay than of a "point landing" at 3.0 percent on the deficit criterion.

"Those of us in industry know that three is not necessarily 3.0," Focus quoted Bayerische Vereinsbank chairman Albrecht Schmidt as saying, adding that a deficit of 3.1 percent or 3.3 percent posed no danger.
